paper_title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (\ours{}), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Generation, imputation, and prediction use different aspects of the same tabular distribution. Generation produces complete records, imputation recovers missing features from observed information, and prediction infers designated target. Each task has its own benchmarks and modeling traditions (Yang et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2025; Erickson et al., 2025), yet their common statistical foundation suggests opportunities for sharing learned capabilities. Understanding these relationships matters for building models that can serve several uses of table, and for deciding when task should benefit from training on another. The conditional-query view makes this connection explicit: generation queries the joint distribution, while imputation and prediction query feature and target conditionals. Models increasingly support several of these interfaces (Ivanov et al., 2019; Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024; Zhang et al., *Equal contribution. Corresponding authors. 1 Figure 1: OTBench overview. (a) Benchmark datasets and fixed traintest splits shared across tasks. (b) Query contracts specify the observed and queried cells for generation, imputation, and prediction. (c) Complementary analyses assess rank alignment, causal transfer under matched objective interventions, and fixed-method generality. Imputation is target-observed for rank alignment (MCAR, 30% missingness) and fixed-method generality (averaged over 12 settings), and targethidden for causal transfer. (d) The reusable suite bundles benchmark definitions, evaluation protocols, code, and configurations. 2025b), but existing task-wise evaluations provide limited insight into which capabilities are shared. Appendix reviews related benchmarks and generalist models. Similar rankings may reflect useful common information without showing whether one training objective helps another. Conversely, objectives that help separately may provide overlapping or competing benefits when combined. We therefore study three questions: which capabilities co-occur across tasks, how objective additions and combinations affect recipient task, and whether one fixed model can offer competitive three-task profile. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (OTBENCH), unified platform for these comparisons. It covers 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 semantic capability axes. common outer train test split aligns the data populations across tasks, while explicit information-access and missingness contracts preserve each tasks meaning. Metric analysis separates point accuracy, distributional fidelity, dependence preservation, predictive quality, and downstream utility, so that cross-task relationships can be located at the level of capabilities. Figure 1 summarizes the benchmark workflow. We first compare task ranks on aligned methoddataset support (Section 4). Imputation and prediction agree most consistently through numerical recovery, dependence preservation, and predictive utility. Generation connects to both through the predictive utility of synthetic data, whereas distributional fidelity has different, sometimes opposing, rank relationships. This suggests that the information needed for useful conditional queries can be shared even when broader distributional criteria favor different methods. To examine objective contributions under controlled changes, we train five backbones under all seven non-empty combinations of generation, imputation, and prediction on five datasets with three seeds 2 and declared inference policies (Section 5). Single-addition effects (SAE) measure the gain from enabling one objective; cross-addition effects (CAE) measure whether two objectives contribute additively. Recipient self-inclusion yields the largest pooled gains. Generation has broadly positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility. These pooled auxiliary responses are descriptive and backbone-dependent. CAE reveals sub-additivity and context dependence on the benchmark rank scale: useful individual objectives need not yield additive joint gains. Finally, fixed-model profiles and comparisons with declared specialist portfolios connect these relationships to practical model choice (Section 6). Fidelity and utility favor different profiles; no fixed identity leads throughout. Recent tabular foundation models (Zhang et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Grinsztajn et al., 2026) achieve strong prediction and numerical point imputation without single-dataset fine-tuning, and their generation is competitive on downstream utility. These results reveal potential for unified foundation models, while motivating better categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling. Our contributions are: conditional-query benchmark that aligns datasets and capability axes across generation, imputation, and prediction while preserving task-specific information and evaluation contracts; Complementary rank comparisons, matched objective interventions, and fixed-model profile experiments that distinguish shared capabilities, objective interactions, and practical generality; Empirical findings on utility-centered task relationships, non-additive objective effects, and the potential of foundation models to support all three tasks.

sections.title: 4 TASK RANK ANALYSIS
sections.content: 4.1 OBJECTIVE AND METHOD To characterize cross-task alignment among existing methods, we compare their relative rankings across generation (G), imputation (I), and prediction (P). Consistent rankings would indicate that the evaluated capabilities covary across tasks, whereas axis-dependent or conflicting rankings would show that cross-task performance cannot be adequately summarized by single score. Training protocol. Cross-task rank analysis requires method to support multiple tasks. We therefore select models with benchmark interfaces for at least two of G, I, and P; Table 7 lists the methods and their supported tasks. Each model follows its default training or adaptation protocol, including its prescribed pretrained or in-context route where applicable. Dataset-specific fitting and adaptation use the training split of each OTBENCH dataset, and evaluation uses its held-out test split. The same outer split is shared across tasks, so task comparisons do not change the underlying training and test populations. Appendix G.1 gives the model configurations. For each task pair and b, we identify the common method pool Mab, align metric directions, average scores over seeds or replicates, and analyze classification and regression separately. Imputation uses the target-observed, missing-completely-at-random (MCAR) setting (Rubin, 1976) with missing rate of 0.3. Capability-axis scores follow the common-support rank protocol in Section 3.1. For each axis pair c, and dataset d, we retain methods in Mab for which all declared members of both axes are valid. We orient the metrics and compute percentile ranks on this aligned method set, then aggregate the member ranks according to Equation 1. The ranking reference set is specific to each task pair and axis pair. We compute one pooled Spearman correlation (Spearman, 1904) over the aligned datasetmethod units. To assess sensitivity to method-pool composition, we perform leave-one-method-out (LOMO) analysis by removing each method in turn and recomputing the aligned support, within-dataset ranks, axis scores, and pooled correlation. An axis pair is LOMO-direction-preserving only when every effective deletion preserves the sign of the full-pool correlation; deletions that change no valid unit are excluded from this diagnostic. Appendix gives the full construction. 4.2 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Cross-task rank agreement depends on the capability axes being compared (Figure 2). No uniform correspondence holds across all tasks and evaluation dimensions. Imputationprediction. Imputation and prediction show selective rank agreement, with 13 of the 24 classification axis pairs and 14 of the 18 regression pairs preserving direction under LOMO. G, I, P-cls, and P-reg denote generation, imputation, classification prediction, and regression prediction. both prediction settings, numerical point accuracy, association, and downstream utility gap have positive, direction-preserving correlations with every prediction axis. The distributional axes show different pattern. Numerical distribution maintains positive agreement with all three regression axes, but neither distribution axis has direction-preserving relationship with classification performance. Recovering values for individual records and preserving variable relationships can retain information useful for target prediction. This is consistent with our intuition that learned statistical dependencies can support both imputation and prediction. Matching marginal value distributions emphasizes different property of the completed data, which helps explain its less uniform correspondence with prediction. The connection is more direct for downstream utility gap because it evaluates completion quality through predictive performance. Together, these results locate the shared performance of imputation and prediction in numerical recovery, dependence preservation, and predictive utility. For unified models, this suggests focus on learning relationships that support both missing-feature recovery and target prediction, including when the target itself is unavailable as conditioning information. Generationimputation. Generation and imputation have the highest proportion of LOMOdirection-preserving relationships among the task pairs, with 36 of the 42 axis pairs preserving direction. TSTR gap and global-utility compromise show positive, direction-preserving correlations with all six imputation axes. Privacy-risk diagnostics show negative, direction-preserving correlations with every imputation axis except numerical distribution. TSTR gap measures the preservation of target-specific predictive utility relative to predictors trained on real data. Its positive rank correlations indicate that generation methods whose synthetic data better preserve this utility also tend to rank higher on imputation. This is consistent with our intuition that learned variable dependencies can support both useful data generation and missing-value recovery. Fidelity and C2ST assess marginal and low-order statistical similarity and realsynthetic distinguishability, respectively, and their correlations with imputation axes vary in sign. Thus, both tasks can use dependencies among table variables, but method that ranks highly on generation metrics does not necessarily lead on imputation. Whether its advantage carries over depends on how effectively the learned relationships support recovery of missing values from observed information. Generationprediction. For generation and prediction, 17 of the 28 classification axis pairs and 9 of the 21 regression axis pairs preserve direction under LOMO. Fidelity and C2ST show negative, direction-preserving correlations with all four classification axes, whereas TSTR gap and global-utility 6 compromise show positive, direction-preserving correlations with all classification and regression axes. This contrast in correlation signs distinguishes the statistical similarity of synthetic data from their predictive utility. Prediction relies on conditional information relevant to specified target, while generation evaluation also examines other distributional properties whose importance to that target can vary. The shared focus of TSTR gap and the prediction axes on target-related information helps explain their positive rank agreement. These results connect generation and prediction through the preservation of target-specific predictive utility. Future work could explicitly model target-relevant dependencies in generation and assess their effects on predictive utility and distributional fidelity.

This reveals which capabilities tend to co-occur across methods, but leaves open how the tasks contribute to one another within model: architectures, training protocols, and objective combinations vary together in those comparisons. To examine these relationships under controlled changes, we ask whether adding an objective improves another recipient task, and whether objectives combine additively within shared model. We call this experiment causal transfer: matched interventions on the enabled objectives complement the observational evidence from task ranks. Experimental setup and evaluation. We train Gaussian Copula (Patki et al., 2016), ForestVP Joint (Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024), TabDiff (Shi et al., 2025), TabSyn (Zhang et al., 2024), and TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., 2023) under all seven non-empty objective arms = {G, I, P, GI, GP, IP, GIP }. The study uses five datasetsJapaneseVowels, cleveland, credit card clients default, website phishing, and MiamiHousing2016and training seeds {0, 1, 2}, yielding 525 backbonedatasetseedarm systems. The first four datasets are classification problems and the last is regression. We use the fixed OTBENCH training and test splits, hold the configured training budget fixed across arms within each backbone, and sample enabled objectives uniformly during fitting. scores all table variables; reconstructs randomly selected features with the target hidden; predicts the target from the features. sections.title: 6 FIXED-METHOD GENERALITY
sections.content: We now compare fixed model identities across tasks and ask when one generalist is competitive with specialist portfolio. Each method retains the same identity across datasets, capability axes, and missingness settings. Comparisons preserve the task contracts and percentile composites in Equation 1; no method switches identities to assemble an oracle. Performance rankings depend on the capability axis. Figure 7 reports the fraction of contractcompatible fixed specialists beaten by each generalist, averaged over paired datasets with half credit for ties. Imputation comparisons are computed separately in each of the twelve target-observed mechanismrate settings before averaging. These fractions describe relative position, not raw accuracy. Generation shows clear separation between distributional fidelity and predictive utility: Gaussian Copula leads fidelity, C2ST, and α-precision, Forest-VP Joint leads association, and TabPFN-3 leads the TSTR-gap axis and global-utility composite. Imputation is similarly divided: TabPFN3 leads numerical point accuracy, TabICLv2 leads numerical distribution, association, and utility preservation, and TabSyn leads both categorical axes. LimiX-2 leads every displayed prediction axis. Thus, competence on one criterion does not imply matching advantage on other criteria, even within the same task. Figure 7: generalists advantage is capability-specific. Cells are mean fractions of fixed specialists beaten on each axis. Panels show (a) generation, (b) imputation averaged over twelve separately evaluated settings, and (c) prediction. Columns are not pooled into leaderboard. Joint profiles expose different bottlenecks and trade-offs. Figure 8(a)(c) connects each methods G, I, and coordinates under three prespecified profiles. Numerical fidelity combines generation fidelity, numerical imputation point accuracy, and regression squared error; categorical fidelity substitutes categorical imputation point accuracy and classification hard decisions; downstream utility combines generation TSTR, imputation utility preservation, and classification hard decisions. Each profile uses its own common dataset cohort. Its percentile-composite coordinates differ from the specialist-beating fractions in Figure 7. High prediction and numerical imputation can coexist with weaker generation fidelity, while several generative methods show the opposite imbalance. Categorical reconstruction introduces another bottleneck, and the utility profile produces different, often more balanced ordering. These contrasts show why single cross-task average would obscure useful distinctions. The practical Pareto frontier (ϵ = .05) contains LimiX-2 and TabDDPM for numerical fidelity; Gaussian Copula, TabDDPM, TabDiff, and TabPFN-3 for categorical fidelity; and LimiX-2, TabDDPM, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3 for utility. No fixed identity is uniformly best across the three profiles. Figure 8: Fixed identities show profile-dependent deployment trade-offs. Panels (a)(c) connect G, I, and percentiles for numerical fidelity, categorical fidelity, and utility on 12, 3, and 26 common datasets. Green and yellow rows indicate practical and exact-only frontiers. Panels (d)(f) show generalist-minus-fixed-portfolio gaps in worst-task percentile on 11, 3, and 26 common datasets, with bootstrap intervals and gray .05 band. Positive gaps favor the generalist. Specialist portfolios retain fidelity advantage. Figure 8(d)(f) compares each generalist with one declared specialist triple per profile (Appendix F.3), using paired differences in worst-task percentile. The numerical-fidelity portfolio outperforms every generalist. The categorical portfolio also has higher mean performance throughout: generalist-minus-portfolio gaps range from .396 to .261, with all bootstrap intervals below zero, although this cohort contains only three datasets. Utility yields different conclusion. TabICLv2 exceeds its portfolio by .157 (95% CI [.078, .229]) and TabPFN-3 by .142 ([.051, .227]). LimiX-2s interval spans zero, while the remaining methods have negative mean gaps. Generalist deployment is therefore most competitive for the evaluated utility profile; fidelity-oriented workloads continue to benefit from specialization. Appendix gives the setting-specific comparisons and statistical diagnostics. Implications for foundation models. LimiX-2, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3 achieve strong numerical point imputation and prediction without single-dataset fine-tuning, while their generation is more competitive on utility than fidelity. LimiX-2 includes masked-feature reconstruction, whereas TabICLv2 and TabPFN-3 reuse pretrained predictors through conditional imputation extensions (Zhang 12 et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Grinsztajn et al., 2026; Prior Labs, 2026). Categorical reconstruction on the common profile cohort and faithful joint generation remain limitations. Amid rapid progress and growing interest in tabular foundation models, these findings highlight their potential across all three tasks. We hope our results encourage foundation-model researchers to develop unified model that excels at generation, imputation, and prediction.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: OTBENCH provides common setting for studying how generation, imputation, and prediction relate through their capabilities, training objectives, and fixed-model performance. Task-rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility. Distributional fidelity follows different relationships, so task competence cannot be inferred from one criterion alone. Matched objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from recipient self-inclusion and suggest backbone-dependent auxiliary benefits from generation and prediction. Their benefits need not add: joint outcomes depend on the recipient and the objectives already present. Fixed-model profiles further show why utility and fidelity can favor different generalist or specialist choices. Foundation models already demonstrate strong prediction and numerical point imputation without dataset-specific fine-tuning, together with promising synthetic-data utility. Amid rapid progress in this field, these findings highlight their potential across all three tasks. We hope OTBENCH encourages researchers to develop foundation models that excel at generation, imputation, and prediction, including reliable categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

sections.title: 8 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Scope and comparability. Our conclusions depend on the capability axes, information contracts, and available methoddataset support. Rank alignment describes capability co-occurrence, rather than identifying objective transfer. In particular, the rank studys target-observed imputation and the controlled studys target-hidden imputation provide complementary evidence under different contracts. Profile and portfolio comparisons also use different common cohorts; the categorical profile contains only three datasets. Cross-task imputation coordinates average twelve settings and do not replace setting-specific evaluation. Objective effects and their mechanisms. The factorial study covers five backbones and five datasets, with only one regression dataset and some unavailable evaluations. Auxiliary single-addition effects remain exploratory and heterogeneous across backbones. SAE and CAE quantify changes on normalized rank scale; they do not identify the mechanisms behind those changes. I/P selfinclusion and some interaction comparisons can also change the conditioning policy, while fixed training budgets redistribute updates among objectives. Objective overlap, update allocation, capacity competition, and gradient interference therefore require separate interventions. Directions for unified models. The frozen foundation-model results establish the capabilities of the evaluated inference systems, without isolating the contribution of pretraining, representations, or decoders. Matched pretraining and inference ablations are needed before attributing categorical or generation gaps to specific backbone properties. Future work should broaden the dataset and model populations, separate training from inference effects, and test how categorical reconstruction and joint sampling can improve alongside prediction.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: To facilitate reproducibility, we describe the task definitions in Section 2 and the evaluation and aggregation protocols in Section 3. Dataset sources, selection criteria, data splits, and preprocessing procedures are detailed in Appendix A. Baseline configurations, hyperparameter settings and selection rules, random seeds, and computational resources are provided in Appendix G. Metric definitions and result aggregation procedures are specified in Appendices and C, with analysis-specific protocols in Appendices DF. Benchmark source code, method configurations, and evaluation routines are publicly available at https://github.com/limix-ldm-ai/OTBench.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This study evaluates tabular learning methods using publicly available datasets under their respective licenses and terms of use. We do not collect additional personal data or attempt to identify individuals in the datasets. We recognize that synthetic data may retain sensitive information from the training data, and that empirical privacy evaluations do not constitute formal privacy guarantees. Furthermore, aggregate benchmark performance does not establish fairness across demographic groups or suitability for deployment in high-stakes settings. Any downstream use should therefore be accompanied by application-specific assessments of privacy, fairness, and reliability.

sections.content: A.1 CONSTRUCTION OBJECTIVE AND OVERALL PIPELINE The benchmark supports prediction, missing-value imputation, and data generation under controlled computational budget. Evaluating every candidate dataset would be costly and would overrepresent sources with multiple versions and groups of structurally similar datasets. We therefore select representative datasets using only method-independent dataset properties and fixed landmarking statistics (Pfahringer et al., 2000). All selection rules and configurations are specified before method evaluation begins, so no evaluated methods performance influences dataset selection. The OpenML track uses prespecified size constraints, meta-feature representation, and clustering to obtain 50 representative datasets. The 6 SCM datasets form separate structural evaluation track. A.2 LITERATURE-DRIVEN CANDIDATE DATASET POOL We identify candidate datasets from 24 deduplicated literature source groups. These sources cover general tabular prediction benchmarks as well as specialized studies of missing-value imputation, data generation, structural fidelity, and robustness. Table 4 lists these sources. ForestDiffusion covers both generation and imputation and is counted once; the two relevant TALENT studies form one source group. Literature sources define only the candidate pool and do not determine the weights used for representative selection. After normalizing dataset names and common aliases, we resolve dataset identities using Dataset IDs reported in papers or official configurations, Task IDs that can be mapped to specific versions, frozen identifiers in official benchmark suites, and metadata that agree in dataset name, size, task type, and original source. We merge references to the same Dataset ID across studies while retaining all source attributions. Records with the same name but different Dataset IDs, versions, or sizes are not merged automatically. This process yields 492 datasets with unambiguous OpenML Dataset IDs (Vanschoren et al., 2013). Table 3 in the main text specifies their exact metric membership. This appendix describes the audit protocol and task-specific evidence for these choices. Appendix B.2 defines the metrics displayed in the two rank-correlation figures. For both generation and imputation, the mixed-type association matrix uses for numerical numerical pairs, Cramers for categoricalcategorical pairs (Cramer, 1946), and the correlation ratio η for mixed pairs (Pearson, 1905). The two tasks use different scalar summaries of this shared representation: generation reports the mean absolute difference over comparable off-diagonal pairs and its complement, whereas imputation reports the relative Frobenius distance. The metrics compare the same pairwise dependence representation but are not numerically interchangeable. C.1 AUDIT PROTOCOL: COMMON-SUPPORT RANKS BEFORE CORRELATIONS After constructing the ranks in Equation 1, the pairwise audit retains only cells in which both quantities are observed, discards strata in which either metric is constant, requires at least three methods per stratum and at least 30 paired cells over six datasets, and computes the Pearson correlation of the pooled rank pairs (the Spearman-equivalent construction used by the audit). The catalog sets ak = 0.5 for C2ST and distance-MIA AUROC and ak = 0 for utility gaps. The catalog marks normalized median Gower DCR as neutral; analyses that require direction use the explicit provisional target-one transform 1 and do not promote it to confirmatory privacy evidence. For the spectral audit, is the fixed metric cohort. The strata are dataset for generation, datasetmissingness settingrate contract for imputation, and datasettask type for prediction. Confidence intervals use 500 bootstrap resamples (Efron, 1979) with whole datasets as the resampling units. For relationships with finite confidence intervals, we call pair redundancy candidate only when its oriented correlation satisfies ρ 0.85 and the 95% dataset-bootstrap lower bound is at least 0.70. Conversely, ρ 0.50 with an upper bound at most 0.20 marks stable trade-off. These thresholds inform, but do not replace, semantic judgment. For the cluster counts in Table 2, we apply average linkage to 1 ρ and cut at 0.15. This absolute-correlation clustering detects both duplicate orderings and two-sided trade-offs; only the former can be pruned. The heatmap ordering instead uses signed distance 1 ρ so that opposing directions remain visually separate. The orderings in Figures 12 and 13 display the empirical blocks; adjacency alone does not justify merging metrics. Figures 12 and 13 show the larger generation metric space separately from imputation and prediction to keep individual rank correlations legible. C.2 FROM CORRELATION BLOCKS TO REDUNDANCY CLUSTERS Figures 12 and 13 inform metric selection. Within each task, positive block supports pooling only when its metrics share an estimand; weakly aligned metrics are not pruned and can share named construct only as reportable complementary probes; mixed-sign blocks are retained as explicit trade-offs. The following decisions account for each pooled family and retained direction in Table 3. Generation. The full 29-metric quality audit yields 17 local correlation clusters, the largest number among the three tasks. Figure 12 shows the fixed 20-metric core; the full audit additionally evaluates alternate parameterizations and validity guards. The five marginal/query-fidelity metrics form the clearest positive block: pairwise correlations range from 0.823 to 0.990, and eight of ten pairs pass the conservative redundancy rule. An equivalent shape metric brings the cluster to six. By contrast, the two C2ST variants are only moderately aligned (ρ = 0.599), so linear and nonlinear distinguishability remain separate, reportable probes within the named C2ST axis rather than statistical substitutes. We pool the dense marginal/query block into fidelity, but keep α-precision, association recovery, and TSTR separate because support, dependence, and transfer are not interchangeable with marginal fidelity. sections.title: H RELATED WORK
sections.content: Task-specific models and benchmarks. Generative tabular models span adversarial and variational approaches such as CTGAN and TVAE (Xu et al., 2019), language-model generators such as GReaT (Borisov et al., 2023), and diffusion methods such as TabDDPM, TabSyn, and TabDiff (Kotelnikov et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025). Imputation ranges from chained equations and random forests (van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011; Stekhoven & Buhlmann, 2012) to learned conditional models (Ivanov et al., 2019; Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024). Prediction combines tree ensembles with neural and pretrained models (Chen & Guestrin, 2016; Prokhorenkova et al., 2018; Hollmann et al., 2023). Benchmark suites including Why Trees, TabZilla, TALENT, and TabArena broaden systematic comparisons for prediction (Grinsztajn et al., 2022; McElfresh et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2024; Erickson et al., 2025). These task-wise evaluations establish performance within each problem, while leaving open how capability rankings relate across generation, imputation, and prediction. Generalist and foundation models. Joint-distribution models can support conditional sampling, while arbitrary-conditioning approaches accommodate varied observation patterns (Ivanov et al., 2019; Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024). LimiX further motivates multiple tabular queries within shared modeling framework (Zhang et al., 2025b). Recent tabular foundation models, including LimiX-2, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3 (Zhang et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Grinsztajn et al., 2026), extend the range of pretrained systems considered in our benchmark. Conditional-query extensions also expose generation and imputation routes (Prior Labs, 2026). These developments motivate distinguishing interface coverage from empirical quality under fixed model identities and task contracts. OTBENCH evaluates this distinction through capability-specific scores and joint task profiles, rather than introducing new model architecture. Evaluation and task relations. Synthetic-data quality depends on which aspects of fidelity, dependence, and downstream utility are measured, and metrics can favor conflicting properties (Yang et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2025). Multi-task learning also studies cooperation and competition among training objectives when deciding which tasks to learn together (Standley et al., 2020). OTBENCH connects these issues through three complementary experiments. Task-rank analysis studies capability co-occurrence on aligned support; SAE and CAE measure objective additions and combinations under declared traininginference protocols; and fixed-method profiles compare joint task performance with specialist portfolios. This separates observational task relationships, controlled objective effects, and practical model choice, while preserving information-contract and metric distinctions.
